title: 11. Observability & SRE: Grafana
summary: Grafana is an open-source, multi-source visualization and dashboarding platform that queries dozens of databases (Prometheus, Loki, Elasticsearch, InfluxDB, MySQL, CloudWatch) through a uniform panel-and-dashboard abstraction,…
objectives: What is Grafana's data source abstraction, and why is it the key to Grafana's success?
What are Grafana templating variables, and why are they essential for dashboard maintainability?
Explain Grafana's panel types and when to use each.
How does Grafana provisioning work, and why is it the production-grade way to manage dashboards?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Grafana is an open-source, multi-source visualization and dashboarding platform that queries dozens of databases (Prometheus, Loki, Elasticsearch, InfluxDB, MySQL, CloudWatch) through a uniform panel-and-dashboard abstraction, with templating variables, alerting, and provisioning — it is the de facto visualization layer for cloud-native observability stacks.
Grafana was created in 2014 by Torkel Ödegaard at Orbitz as a fork of Kibana's frontend, motivated by frustration that Kibana was tightly coupled to Elasticsearch and could not visualize Graphite or Prometheus data. The original goal was modest: a single web UI that could query any time-series database and render panels. Over the next decade, Grafana expanded into a multi-source platform that supports more than 150 data source plugins (Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, Elasticsearch, InfluxDB, OpenTSDB, Graphite, MySQL, Postgres, CloudWatch, Azure Monitor, Datadog, Snowflake, ClickHouse, and many more), a templating system that lets one dashboard serve many environments, an alerting engine that routes to PagerDuty/Slack/email, a provisioning system that stores dashboards as code in Git, and an ecosystem of companion products (Loki for logs, Tempo for traces, Mimir for metrics, OnCall for paging) that together form the Grafana Stack. Real-world deployments span CERN (which runs Grafana dashboards across the LHC computing grid), hedge funds (which use Grafana for market-data and trading-system dashboards), Netflix (which uses an internal fork for operational dashboards), and the majority of Kubernetes clusters worldwide — Grafana is the default visualization layer for the Prometheus ecosystem.

The first foundational concept is the data source abstraction. Grafana itself stores no data — it is a query engine and renderer. Every panel in a dashboard is configured with a data source (a connection to a database) and a query (in that database's native query language). When a user opens a dashboard, Grafana fans out the queries to the configured data sources in parallel, receives the responses, normalizes them into a common data frame format (a tabular structure with time column, value columns, and metadata), and renders them as panels. This abstraction is what makes Grafana powerful: the same dashboard can show a Prometheus chart, a Loki log stream, and a MySQL table side by side, with cross-panel linking (click a row in the MySQL table to filter the Prometheus chart by the clicked label). The trade-off is that Grafana cannot use any feature the data source does not expose — it is constrained by the query language and capabilities of the underlying database, which is why Grafana's Prometheus panels use PromQL while its Loki panels use LogQL while its Elasticsearch panels use Lucene.

The second concept is the dashboard-panel hierarchy. A dashboard is a grid of panels, each panel has a visualization type (time series, stat, gauge, table, heatmap, log stream, node graph, geomap, bar chart, pie chart, and more), a query, and a set of transformations (join, filter, group by, calculate delta, sort). Panels can be organized into rows that collapse, can override their time range independently of the dashboard, and can be linked to other dashboards via drill-down links. The dashboard also has templating variables — drop-down selectors at the top that filter every panel's query, so one dashboard serves many environments (`$environment` = prod/staging/dev), many services (`$service` = checkout/payments/search), or many instances (`$instance`). The discipline is to design dashboards that answer one operational question each: a "service overview" dashboard answers "is the service healthy?" with golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation); a "deep-dive" dashboard answers "why is the service slow?" with per-endpoint latency, dependency latency, and resource metrics; a "capacity" dashboard answers "when do we run out?" with utilization trends and forecasts. CERN's dashboard taxonomy formalizes this into "operations," "investigation," and "planning" categories, with strict rules about which panel types belong in each.

The third concept is templating variables. Variables are the mechanism by which one dashboard serves many use cases. A variable like `$service` is defined as a query (`label_values(http_requests_total, service)` in Prometheus, or `SHOW TABLES` in MySQL) that returns the list of distinct values; the variable's current value is substituted into every panel's query (`http_requests_total{service="$service"}`). Variables can be chained — `$region` filters `$cluster` filters `$instance` — so selecting "us-east-1" in the first dropdown populates the second with only us-east-1 clusters. Variables can be text boxes (free-form filters), intervals (used in `rate(...[$__interval])` for auto-binned rates), or custom constants. The discipline is to use variables for everything that varies across deployments: environment, region, cluster, service, instance, route. Without variables, a team ends up with one dashboard per service per environment, which is unmaintainable — with variables, one dashboard serves all of them.

The fourth concept is alerting. Grafana's alerting system, introduced in version 8 (2021) and unified in version 9, lets users define alert rules that query any data source, evaluate on a schedule, and route to notification channels. An alert rule has a query (e.g., `rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) > 0.1`), a condition (above/below threshold for N evaluations), a notification policy (route based on labels — `severity=page` to PagerDuty, `severity=ticket` to Jira, `severity=chat` to Slack), and silencing rules. Grafana Alerting replaces the older "Grafana alerting v1" (per-panel alerts) with a unified model where alerts are first-class objects stored in the database, queryable via API, and managed independently of dashboards. The trade-off versus Prometheus's native alerting is flexibility (Grafana can alert on any data source, not just Prometheus) versus operational integration (Prometheus alerting integrates with Alertmanager's dedup and grouping, which Grafana's alerting must reimplement). Most teams use Prometheus alerting for metric-based alerts and Grafana alerting for cross-source alerts (e.g., "log error rate exceeds threshold" using Loki, or "SQL query returned anomaly" using MySQL).

The fifth concept is provisioning. Grafana stores dashboards, data sources, alert rules, and notification policies in its database by default — but for production reliability, this state should be in version control, not in the database. Grafana's provisioning system lets teams define these resources as YAML files in a directory (`/etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/`, `/etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources/`, `/etc/grafana/provisioning/alerting/`), and Grafana loads them on startup, reconciling the database state to match the files. This enables GitOps workflows: dashboards live in a Git repo, pull requests review dashboard changes, CI/CD deploys the repo to the Grafana instance, and the dashboard state is reproducible from source. Grafana Labs also offers a Terraform provider and a `gcloud`-like CLI (`grafana-cli`) for managing dashboards as code. The discipline is: never edit dashboards in production directly — always edit in a staging instance, export to JSON, commit to Git, deploy to production via provisioning. This is the same pattern as infrastructure-as-code, applied to observability.

The sixth concept is the Grafana ecosystem. Grafana Labs, the company behind Grafana, has built companion products that integrate tightly: Loki (log aggregation, designed for label-based queries like Prometheus but for logs), Tempo (distributed tracing backend, native OpenTelemetry support), Mimir (horizontally-scalable Prometheus-compatible metrics backend, the successor to Cortex), OnCall (pager and on-call schedule management, an alternative to PagerDuty), Alloy (OpenTelemetry-compatible collector), and Faro (frontend observability). The integration is the value: a Grafana dashboard can show a Prometheus metric chart, click a point to see the Loki logs from that time window for that service, click a log line to see the Tempo trace for that request ID, and click a span in the trace to see the relevant logs. This "three pillars in one UI" workflow is what Grafana Labs sells as the Grafana Stack, and it is the open-source alternative to Datadog, New Relic, and Splunk Observability.

The trade-off in Grafana is flexibility versus consistency. Because Grafana supports so many data sources and panel types, it can render almost anything — but it does not enforce any conventions. A team can build a dashboard with inconsistent time ranges, mismatched units, stale queries, and panels that don't quite answer the question. The discipline is to adopt conventions: golden signals dashboards follow the RED/USE frameworks, dashboards are organized by service, every panel has a clear title and unit, every dashboard is provisioned from Git, and dashboards are reviewed in pull requests just like code. Without these conventions, Grafana devolves into a graveyard of stale dashboards that no one trusts.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    U[Engineer opens dashboard]
    U --> G[Grafana server]
    G --> V{Resolve variables}
    V -->|query Prometheus| DS1[(Prometheus / Mimir)]
    V -->|query Loki| DS2[(Loki)]
    V -->|query MySQL| DS3[(MySQL)]
    V -->|query CloudWatch| DS4[(CloudWatch)]
    DS1 --> G
    DS2 --> G
    DS3 --> G
    DS4 --> G
    G --> R[Render panels: timeseries, table, logs, traces]
    R --> U
    G --> A[Alerting engine]
    A -->|eval rules| DS1
    A -->|route| NC[Notification policies]
    NC --> PD[PagerDuty]
    NC --> SL[Slack]
    NC --> EM[Email]
    G --> P[Provisioning: YAML in Git]
    P --> G
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
+--------------------------------------------------+
|  Grafana dashboard  (templated by $service)      |
|  [$service=checkout] [$env=prod] [$region=us-e1] |
|--------------------------------------------------|
|  +-------------+  +-------------+                |
|  | Latency p99 |  | Error rate  |   <-- PromQL   |
|  +-------------+  +-------------+                |
|  +-------------+  +-------------+                |
|  | Throughput  |  | CPU/Mem     |   <-- PromQL   |
|  +-------------+  +-------------+                |
|  +------------------------------------------+    |
|  | Log stream (errors only)   <-- LogQL    |    |
|  +------------------------------------------+    |
|  +------------------------------------------+    |
|  | Trace list (slow reqs)     <-- Tempo    |    |
|  +------------------------------------------+    |
+--------------------------------------------------+
              |  panel queries fan out
              v
   +----------+----------+----------+----------+
   |          |          |          |          |
   v          v          v          v          v
+------+  +-------+  +-------+  +--------+  +-------+
|Prom  |  |Mimir  |  |Loki   |  |Tempo   |  |MySQL  |
|(15d) |  |(1y)   |  |(30d)  |  |(7d)    |  |(live) |
+------+  +-------+  +-------+  +--------+  +-------+

Provisioning (GitOps):
  dashboards/         -> /etc/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/*.yaml
  datasources/        -> /etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources/*.yaml
  alerting/           -> /etc/grafana/provisioning/alerting/*.yaml
  CI/CD: git push -> Grafana reloads -> dashboards in DB match files
```

### Walkthrough
1. The engineer opens a dashboard URL; Grafana resolves the templating variables (queries Prometheus for `label_values(http_requests_total, service)` to populate the `$service` dropdown, etc.) and substitutes the default values into every panel's query.
2. Grafana fans out the queries to the configured data sources in parallel — PromQL to Prometheus/Mimir, LogQL to Loki, TraceQL to Tempo, SQL to MySQL — receiving responses in each source's native format.
3. Grafana normalizes the responses into a common data frame format (time + value columns + metadata), applies any panel transformations (join, filter, group by), and renders each panel as its visualization type (time series, stat, table, log stream, trace list).
4. Clicking a point on a time-series chart can drill through to a correlated view — same time window, same service label — in Loki logs or Tempo traces, giving the engineer a three-pillars workflow without leaving Grafana.
5. Separately, Grafana's alerting engine evaluates rules on a schedule, routes firing alerts to notification channels based on label-matched policies, and the entire dashboard/alert/datasource state is provisioned from YAML files in Git via CI/CD.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# grafana_dashboard_gen.py - runnable; generates a Grafana dashboard JSON
import json, uuid

def panel_timeseries(panel_id: int, title: str, expr: str, grid_x: int, grid_y: int, w=12, h=8):
    return {
        "id": panel_id,
        "type": "timeseries",
        "title": title,
        "gridPos": {"x": grid_x, "y": grid_y, "w": w, "h": h},
        "datasource": {"type": "prometheus", "uid": "prom-1"},
        "targets": [{"refId": "A", "expr": expr, "legendFormat": "{{service}}"}],
        "fieldConfig": {
            "defaults": {"unit": "s", "custom": {"drawStyle": "line", "lineWidth": 1}},
            "overrides": [],
        },
        "options": {"legend": {"displayMode": "table", "placement": "bottom"}},
    }

def panel_stat(panel_id: int, title: str, expr: str, grid_x: int, grid_y: int, w=6, h=4, unit="short"):
    return {
        "id": panel_id, "type": "stat", "title": title,
        "gridPos": {"x": grid_x, "y": grid_y, "w": w, "h": h},
        "datasource": {"type": "prometheus", "uid": "prom-1"},
        "targets": [{"refId": "A", "expr": expr}],
        "fieldConfig": {"defaults": {"unit": unit}, "overrides": []},
        "options": {"reduceOptions": {"calcs": ["lastNotNull"]}},
    }

def panel_logs(panel_id: int, title: str, expr: str, grid_x: int, grid_y: int, w=24, h=8):
    return {
        "id": panel_id, "type": "logs", "title": title,
        "gridPos": {"x": grid_x, "y": grid_y, "w": w, "h": h},
        "datasource": {"type": "loki", "uid": "loki-1"},
        "targets": [{"refId": "A", "expr": expr}],
        "options": {"showTime": True, "showLabels": True, "showCommonLabels": False},
    }

def templating_var(name: str, query: str, label: str, data_source="Prometheus"):
    return {
        "name": name, "label": label, "type": "query",
        "datasource": data_source, "query": query,
        "refresh": 1, "includeAll": True, "multi": False,
        "current": {"text": "All", "value": "$__all"},
    }

def build_service_dashboard(service: str = "$service") -> dict:
    panels = [
        panel_stat(1, "Requests/s",  f'sum(rate(http_requests_total{{service="{service}"}}[5m]))', 0, 0, unit="reqps"),
        panel_stat(2, "Error rate",  f'sum(rate(http_requests_total{{service="{service}",status=~"5.."}}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{{service="{service}"}}[5m]))', 6, 0, unit="percentunit"),
        panel_stat(3, "p99 latency", f'histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{{service="{service}"}}[5m])) by (le))', 12, 0, unit="s"),
        panel_stat(4, "Saturation",  f'avg(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{{service="{service}"}}) * 100', 18, 0, unit="percent"),
        panel_timeseries(5, "Latency percentiles", f'histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{{service="{service}"}}[5m])) by (le))', 0, 4),
        panel_timeseries(6, "Throughput by route", f'sum(rate(http_requests_total{{service="{service}"}}[5m])) by (route)', 12, 4),
        panel_logs(7, "Error logs (last 1h)", '{service="' + service + '"} |= "ERROR"', 0, 12),
    ]
    return {
        "uid": str(uuid.uuid4())[:8],
        "title": f"Service Overview - {service}",
        "tags": ["sre", "service-overview"],
        "timezone": "browser",
        "schemaVersion": 39,
        "version": 1,
        "refresh": "30s",
        "time": {"from": "now-6h", "to": "now"},
        "templating": {"list": [
            templating_var("service", "label_values(http_requests_total, service)", "Service"),
            templating_var("env",     "label_values(http_requests_total, env)",     "Environment"),
        ]},
        "panels": panels,
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    dash = build_service_dashboard("$service")
    print(json.dumps(dash, indent=2)[:1800])
    print("...")
    print(f"\n# dashboard has {len(dash['panels'])} panels, {len(dash['templating']['list'])} variables")
```
